query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The substitution of Ti with a lighter element, such as Al, in the HfMoTaTiZr alloy can reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.conditions: Room temperature and elevated temperatures up to 1000 °C
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a solid solution phase with a body-centered cubic (BCC) structure
generation.mechanism: The substitution of Ti with Al can reduce the density of the alloy while maintaining its mechanical properties due to the formation of a solid solution phase with a BCC structure, which is stable at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The density of the alloy will decrease, while its mechanical properties, such as yield strength and ultimate strength, will remain similar to those of the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
generation.uncertainty: The exact effect of the substitution of Ti with Al on the mechanical properties of the alloy at elevated temperatures is uncertain and requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Compression tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures up to 1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yield strength and ultimate strength of the alloy with Ti substituted by Al are significantly lower than those of the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

In 2004, Professor Yeh and his group published the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) []. He defined high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as having five or more major elements beneath 5–35 at.%, and minor elements below five at.%. In 2006, he also established four core effects of HEAs []: High-entropy, severe-lattices-distortion, sluggish-diffusion, and the cocktail effect. ## 2. Materials and Methods
The experimental Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy series was prepared by vacuum-arc melting. The purity of raw elements including Hf, Mo, Nb, Ta, and Zr was 99.9 wt.%, and that of Ti was 99.99 wt.%. These pure metals were stacked together in the sequence of low melting point to high melting point from bottom to top. The stacked metals were melted together in a water-cool copper mold and solidified therein. The ingot of each alloy was flipped and re-melted, at least, four times to improve the chemical homogeneity.
